questions.title: Mathematical Literacy concepts, hexagonal paving bricks and a fold-up beach chair

subQuestions.questionText:
TABLE 1 below contains a list of explanations and definitions of concepts used in Mathematical Literacy.

**TABLE 1: EXPLANATIONS AND DEFINITIONS OF CONCEPTS**

| Letter | Explanation or definition |
|---|---|
| A | A measuring system using metres, litres and kilograms |
| B | The amount of space occupied by an object |
| C | A system measuring in inches, gallons and pounds |
| D | The amount of space available to hold something |
| E | The side of a building you see when you are facing south |
| F | The side of a building you see when you are facing north |
| G | The amount of space that is enclosed by the perimeter of an object |

Use TABLE 1 above and match an explanation or a definition with the concept below. Write only the letter (A–G).

**Capacity**
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **D** — The amount of space available to hold something (2A correct option)
Teaching point: Capacity is how much a container can HOLD (measured in litres, millilitres, etc.). Do not confuse it with volume (option B), which is the amount of space an object itself OCCUPIES.

**North elevation**
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **E** — The side of a building you see when you are facing south (2A correct option)
Teaching point: An elevation is named after the compass direction that the wall FACES. The north elevation faces north, so you must stand to the north of the building and look southwards to see it.

Teaching point: Area is the flat space INSIDE the boundary (perimeter) of a two-dimensional shape, measured in square units such as $\text{cm}^2$ or $\text{m}^2$.

subQuestions.questionText:
Paving bricks are available in different shapes and sizes. Hexagonal paving bricks are made up of 6 equal triangles and will be used to cover a rectangular ground surface.

**DIMENSIONS OF THE HEXAGONAL PAVING BRICK**

| Dimension | Measurement |
|---|---|
| Equal side lengths (L) | 90 mm |
| Height (H) | 50 mm |
| Width (W) | 220 mm |

Convert 220 mm to metres.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $220 \text{ mm} \div 1\,000$ (1MA dividing by 1 000)
Mark 2: $= 0{,}22 \text{ m}$ (1A conversion)
Teaching point: There are 1 000 mm in 1 m, so millimetres $\to$ metres means DIVIDE by 1 000 (the answer must be smaller).

subQuestions.questionText:
A hexagonal paving brick is made up of 6 equal triangles. Its dimensions are:

| Dimension | Measurement |
|---|---|
| Equal side lengths (L) | 90 mm |
| Height (H) | 50 mm |
| Width (W) | 220 mm |

Choose, from the options (A, B or C) below, the correct one that could be used to calculate the volume of the hexagonal paving brick.

A  Volume = 6 × area of triangle × height
B  Volume = side length + height + width
C  Volume = 6 × perimeter × height
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **A** — Volume = 6 × area of triangle × height (2A correct option)
Teaching point: For any prism, Volume = area of the base $\times$ height. The hexagonal base is made up of 6 equal triangles, so the base area is $6 \times$ (area of one triangle). Option B adds lengths (that gives a length, not a volume) and option C uses perimeter (a length), so neither can give a volume.

subQuestions.questionText:
Hexagonal paving bricks will be laid in single rows to cover a rectangular ground surface. The dimensions of ONE paving brick are:

| Dimension | Measurement |
|---|---|
| Equal side lengths (L) | 90 mm |
| Height (H) | 50 mm |
| Width (W) | 220 mm |

When three bricks are placed in a row they touch side by side, so each brick takes up its full width (W) of 220 mm along the row.

Calculate the number of bricks needed for a single row along a length of 2 860 mm.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Number of bricks $= 2\,860 \text{ mm} \div 220 \text{ mm}$ (1RT correct values read from the information)
Mark 2: (1MA dividing)
Mark 3: $= 13$ bricks (1A number of bricks)
Teaching point: To find how many items fit into a length, divide the total length by the length of ONE item. Keep both measurements in the same unit (both in mm here).
subQuestions.topic: Measurement – Number of items along a length

subQuestions.questionText:
The fold-up chair is a beach chair that folds into itself. The material list for ONE chair is given below.

**MATERIAL LIST**

| # (number of items) | Wooden item | Dimensions (in cm) |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | Chair supports | 1,9 × 3,8 × 66 |
| 13 | Crosspieces | 1,9 × 3,8 × 36 |
| 1 | Seat back, bottom crosspiece | 1,9 × 3,8 × 32 |

NOTE:
- The thickness of the wood is the smallest dimension.
- # is the number of item(s).

Write down the total number of wooden items needed to assemble this chair.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: $4 + 13 + 1 = 18$ wooden items (2A correct number)
Teaching point: The column headed # gives how many of each item are needed — simply add the three quantities.
subQuestions.topic: Number sense – Reading and adding from a table

subQuestions.questionText:
The fold-up beach chair is made from 4 chair supports, 13 crosspieces and 1 seat back / bottom crosspiece.

The crosspieces are shared between the seat and the back of the chair. On the 3D sketch of ONE assembled chair, **6 crosspieces** are fitted across the SEAT of the chair (the remaining crosspieces form the back).

Determine the number of crosspieces found on the seats of THREE chairs.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: 6 crosspieces on the seat of ONE chair (1RT reading 6 from the sketch)
Mark 2: Number of crosspieces $= 6 \times 3$ (1A multiplying by 3)
Mark 3: $= 18$ crosspieces (1A pieces)
Teaching point: Read the number for ONE chair first, then multiply by the number of chairs.

subQuestions.questionText:
The material list for the fold-up beach chair is given below.

**MATERIAL LIST**

| # (number of items) | Wooden item | Dimensions (in cm) |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | Chair supports | 1,9 × 3,8 × 66 |
| 13 | Crosspieces | 1,9 × 3,8 × 36 |
| 1 | Seat back, bottom crosspiece | 1,9 × 3,8 × 32 |

Name the item in the material list with the longest dimension.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **Chair support** (2RT correct option)
Teaching point: Compare the largest dimension of each item: 66 cm (chair support), 36 cm (crosspiece) and 32 cm (seat back / bottom crosspiece). 66 cm is the biggest, so the chair support is the longest item.

subQuestions.questionText:
In the material list of the fold-up beach chair, the chair support has dimensions **1,9 × 3,8 × 66** (in cm).

NOTE: The thickness of the wood is the smallest dimension.

Identify which dimension of the chair support will represent the thickness of the wood.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **1,9 cm** (2A correct dimension; NPU — no penalty for omitting the unit)
Teaching point: The note tells you the thickness is the SMALLEST of the three dimensions. Of 1,9 cm, 3,8 cm and 66 cm, the smallest is 1,9 cm.

subQuestions.questionText:
The side view of the fold-up beach chair shows the chair back and the chair seat. On the chair back the gap (spacing) between two crosspieces is labelled as **1,27 cm**.

Write down, in millimetres, the length of the spacing between the crosspieces of the back of the chair.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Spacing $= 1{,}27 \times 10 \text{ mm}$ (1RT correct value read from the side view)
Mark 2: $= 12{,}7 \text{ mm}$ (1MCA simplification; NPU)
Teaching point: 1 cm = 10 mm, so centimetres $\to$ millimetres means MULTIPLY by 10.

questions.title: Baviaanskloof Uitspan camping site and the Leopard Trail Run elevation maps

subQuestions.questionText:
John and five other family members decided to participate in the Baviaanskloof Leopard Trail Run. They decided to camp at the Baviaanskloof Uitspan camping site.

ANNEXURE A shows an **aerial view** of Baviaanskloof Uitspan with the campsites and the number of campers allowed. Some campsites have one hut and others have more than one hut, labelled A, B and C.

Explain what is meant by *aerial view*.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: Any ONE of the following (2A correct explanation):
- A view from the top.
- A view of the landscape from a certain height above the ground, e.g. from a satellite or a drone.
- A view from an elevated height.
- A bird's-eye view.
Teaching point: An aerial view is a photograph or drawing taken looking straight DOWN on a place from above, so you see the layout of the whole site rather than the sides of the buildings.

subQuestions.questionText:
ANNEXURE A shows an aerial view of the Baviaanskloof Uitspan camping site. Some campsites have one hut and others have more than one hut, labelled A, B and C. The number of campers allowed per hut is given below.

**CAMPSITES AND NUMBER OF CAMPERS**

| Campsite / hut | Number of campers |
|---|---|
| Campsite 1 | 6 |
| Campsite 2A | 15 |
| 2B | 4 |
| Campsite 3A | 15 |
| 3B | 4 |
| 3C | 4 |
| Campsite 4 | 5 |
| Campsite 5A | 15 |
| 5B | 8 |
| Campsite 6 | 10 |
| Campsite 7 | 4 – 6 |
| Campsite 8 | 4 – 6 |
| Campsite 9 | 20 |

Calculate the maximum number of campers that can be accommodated at Baviaanskloof Uitspan camping site.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Number of campers $= 6 + 15 + 4 + 15 + 4 + 4 + 5 + 15 + 8 + 10 + 6 + 6 + 20$ (1RT all correct values)
Mark 2: (1MCA adding the values)
Mark 3: $= 118$ campers (1CA simplification; AO — answer only gets full marks)

OR

Mark 1: $= 20 + 15(3) + 10 + 8 + 6(3) + 5 + 4(3)$ (1RT all correct values)
Mark 2: (1MCA adding the values)
Mark 3: $= 118$ campers (1CA simplification)

Teaching point: 'Maximum' means you must use the TOP value of each range, so campsites 7 and 8 each count as 6 campers, not 4.

subQuestions.questionText:
ANNEXURE A shows an aerial view of the Baviaanskloof Uitspan camping site. North is towards the TOP of the aerial view.

On the aerial view:
- The Houkloof mountains run along the northern edge of the site.
- **Campsite 8** lies in the far north-east of the site, in the upper part of the view, with campsites 7, 6, 5, 4 and 3 (and the ablution block) below and to the left of it.
- The **dam** lies well below campsite 8 and towards the left-hand (western) side of the view, with campsites 1, 2 and 9 around it.
- The main house is on the far right of the view.

Determine the general direction of the dam from campsite 8.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **South West / SW** (2A compass direction)
Teaching point: Always start AT the place named after 'from' (campsite 8) and describe where the other place lies. On a map north is up, south is down, east is right and west is left — the dam is both below (south) and to the left (west) of campsite 8, so the direction is south-west.

subQuestions.questionText:
ANNEXURE A shows an aerial view of the Baviaanskloof Uitspan camping site. Campsites 1, 2 and 9 lie closest to the dam. Some campsites have more than one hut, labelled A, B and C.

**CAMPSITES AND NUMBER OF CAMPERS**

| Campsite / hut | Number of campers |
|---|---|
| Campsite 1 | 6 |
| Campsite 2A | 15 |
| 2B | 4 |
| Campsite 3A | 15 |
| 3B | 4 |
| 3C | 4 |
| Campsite 4 | 5 |
| Campsite 5A | 15 |
| 5B | 8 |
| Campsite 6 | 10 |
| Campsite 7 | 4 – 6 |
| Campsite 8 | 4 – 6 |
| Campsite 9 | 20 |

The description below is found on their website:

'This campsite is situated near the dam and can accommodate a maximum of 19 campers.'

Write down which campsite is being described. Write down only the number of the campsite.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: Campsite **2** (2O identifying the correct site)
Teaching point: Campsite 2 has TWO huts, so you must add them together: $15 (\text{2A}) + 4 (\text{2B}) = 19$ campers. Campsite 2 also lies right next to the dam, which matches the rest of the description.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Interpreting a site plan

subQuestions.questionText:
John and five other family members (a family group of SIX people) are camping at Baviaanskloof Uitspan. The camping site has 13 huts in total, and the number of campers each hut can take is given below.

**CAMPSITES AND NUMBER OF CAMPERS**

| Campsite / hut | Number of campers |
|---|---|
| Campsite 1 | 6 |
| Campsite 2A | 15 |
| 2B | 4 |
| Campsite 3A | 15 |
| 3B | 4 |
| 3C | 4 |
| Campsite 4 | 5 |
| Campsite 5A | 15 |
| 5B | 8 |
| Campsite 6 | 10 |
| Campsite 7 | 4 – 6 |
| Campsite 8 | 4 – 6 |
| Campsite 9 | 20 |

Calculate, as a percentage, the probability of John and his family randomly selecting a hut that can exactly accommodate the whole family.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Numerator $= 3$ huts that can take exactly 6 campers — campsite 1 (6), campsite 7 (4 – 6) and campsite 8 (4 – 6) (1A correct numerator)
Mark 2: Denominator $= 13$ huts in total (1A correct denominator)
Mark 3: $P = \dfrac{3}{13} \times 100\% = 23{,}076923\%$ (1CA simplification; NPR)
Teaching point: Probability $= \dfrac{\text{number of favourable outcomes}}{\text{total number of outcomes}}$. Multiply by 100% to express it as a percentage. Campsites 7 and 8 count because a range of 4 – 6 includes exactly 6.

subQuestions.label: 2.1.6 (a)
subQuestions.questionText:
The layout plan of the ablution facilities (toilets and showers) in the middle of campsites 3, 4, 5 and 6 shows the following, reading the plan from the top down:

- Along the **top wall**: a row of NINE identical cubicles, each marked with the shower symbol from the key.
- Along the **left-hand side and lower-left**: two long benches (marked with the bench symbol).
- Along the **bottom right**: a row of SIX cubicles, each marked with the toilet symbol from the key.
- A door opening is shown on the right-hand wall.

**KEY:** shower symbol, toilet symbol, bench symbol.

Write down the total number of showers.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **9 showers** (2A correct number)
Teaching point: Use the KEY to identify which symbol means 'shower', then count only those cubicles on the plan — do not count the toilets or the benches.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Reading a layout plan

subQuestions.label: 2.1.6 (b)
subQuestions.questionText:
The layout plan of the ablution facilities at the camping site is drawn with the overall length of the building shown by an arrow labelled **8,2 m**.

The actual length of the ablution facilities is 8,2 metres. On the printed layout plan this same length **measures 90 mm (9 cm)**.

Determine, rounded to the nearest whole number, the scale of the plan.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Measured distance on the plan $= 90 \text{ mm}$, which represents $8{,}2 \text{ m}$ (1A measured distance)
Mark 2: $8{,}2 \text{ m} = 8\,200 \text{ mm}$ (1C converting to mm)
Mark 3: $90 : 8\,200 \;(\div\, 90)$ (1M dividing by 90)
Mark 4: $= 1 : 91{,}11\ldots \approx \mathbf{1 : 91}$ (1R rounded answer)

OR

Mark 1: $9 \text{ cm} : 8{,}2 \text{ m}$ (1A measured distance)
Mark 2: $9 \text{ cm} : 820 \text{ cm}$ (1C converting to cm)
Mark 3: $\div\, 9$ (1M dividing by 9)
Mark 4: $= 1 : 91{,}11\ldots \approx \mathbf{1 : 91}$ (1R rounded answer)

Note: Accept a deviation of $\pm 1$ mm on the measurement.
Teaching point: A scale is written as (plan length) : (real length) with BOTH lengths in the SAME unit, then simplified so that the plan side equals 1.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Calculating a scale

subQuestions.label: 2.1.6 (c)
subQuestions.questionText:
The layout plan of the ablution facilities at the Baviaanskloof Uitspan camping site shows nine showers along the top wall, six toilets along the bottom right, and TWO long benches along the left-hand side of the building.

Give ONE suitable reason why benches are found in the ablution facilities.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: Any ONE suitable reason (2O reason), for example:
- To allow people to sit while waiting for a toilet or shower to become available.
- To place your clothes or belongings on while you are showering.
- To sit on while you change your outfit / get dressed / apply body lotion.
- To use as a surface for changing a baby's nappy.
Teaching point: An 'opinion' question still needs an answer that fits the CONTEXT — link the bench to something a camper actually does in an ablution block.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Interpretation in context

subQuestions.questionText:
The Leopard Trail Run is a two-day event, run on the outskirts of the camp, starting and ending at the Cedar Falls Home Base.

On the map of the Leopard Trail Run route the Cedar Falls Home Base is in the middle, with the two loops on either side:

| Day | Landmarks shown on that loop |
|---|---|
| Day 1 (loop to the east of the home base) | The Cauldron, Birdsong Valley, Fond Farewell, Honeybush Hill, Inconvenient Truth |
| Day 2 (loop to the west of the home base) | Rhebok Valley, Gabriel's Pools, Reflection Pools |

Write down the day during the run when you would pass Gabriel's Pools.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **Day 2** (2A correct description)
Teaching point: Find the landmark named in the question on the route map and read off which day's loop it lies on. Gabriel's Pools appears on the western loop, which is labelled Day 2.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Reading a route map

subQuestions.questionText:
The Leopard Trail Run is a two-day event starting and ending at the Cedar Falls Home Base. Each day's run is made up of two parts: the runners go out from the home base (Part 1) and then return to the home base (Part 2).

| Day | Landmarks shown on that loop |
|---|---|
| Day 1 (eastern loop) | The Cauldron, Birdsong Valley, Fond Farewell, Honeybush Hill, Inconvenient Truth |
| Day 2 (western loop) | Rhebok Valley (at the far western end), Gabriel's Pools, Reflection Pools (on the way back to the home base) |

The descriptions of a part of the route on the brochure are as follows:

- Run for 5,5 km along Rhebok Valley.
- Continue down the other side to the Reflection Pools for a swim and drinking water.
- Then return to the home base.

Choose the route described above and match it with A, B, C or D.

A  Leopard Trail Run – Day 1 (Part 1)
B  Leopard Trail Run – Day 1 (Part 2)
C  Leopard Trail Run – Day 2 (Part 1)
D  Leopard Trail Run – Day 2 (Part 2)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **D** — Leopard Trail Run – Day 2 (Part 2) (2RT correct option)
Teaching point: Two clues fix the answer. Rhebok Valley and the Reflection Pools are both on the Day 2 loop (so it is Day 2, not Day 1), and the description ends with 'return to the home base', which is the second half of the day's route (Part 2).

subQuestions.questionText:
The elevation map for **Day 2** of the Leopard Trail Run plots the height above sea level (vertical axis) against the distance run (horizontal axis). The horizontal axis is marked at 2,5 km; 5 km; 7,5 km; 10 km; 12,5 km; 15 km; 17,5 km; 20 km and ends at 21,9 km. The vertical axis is labelled 864 m; 900 m; 975 m; 1 050 m and 1 173 m.

Description of the Day 2 profile:
- The trail starts at about 864 m, rises quickly to a small peak just after the start, then runs fairly flat between about 900 m and 975 m up to roughly the 10 km mark.
- From about 10 km it climbs steeply to the **highest point of the whole day, 1 173 m, reached at the 12,5 km mark**.
- It then dips, rises to a second (lower) peak of about 1 050 m at the 17,5 km mark, and finally drops away towards the end of the trail at 21,9 km.

Determine the number of kilometres John had run when he reached the highest point above sea level on Day 2.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **12,5 km** (2RT correct distance)
Teaching point: On an elevation (height) graph, find the highest point on the curve first (1 173 m here), then drop straight DOWN to the horizontal axis to read off the matching distance.
subQuestions.topic: Data handling – Reading an elevation graph

subQuestions.questionText:
The elevation map for **Day 1** of the Leopard Trail Run plots the height above sea level against the distance run. The vertical axis is labelled 721 m, 1 000 m and 1 183 m; the horizontal axis is marked at 5 km; 10 km; 15 km; 20 km; 25 km and ends at 30,5 km (the finish is at 861 m).

Description of the Day 1 profile:
- The trail starts at about 721 m and climbs steeply to a group of sharp peaks reaching 1 183 m between about 5 km and 9 km.
- **From about the 8 km mark the graph falls continuously**, dropping steadily all the way down to the lowest part of the route at about 18 km to 20 km.
- After 22 km it climbs again to about 1 100 m between 23 km and 27 km, before dropping to finish at 861 m at 30,5 km.

John's best average speed (in km/h) for the run was his average speed from the 8 km mark up to the 18 km mark on Day 1.

Use the elevation map to explain why this was the case.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: Any ONE of the following (2O correct explanation):
- That part of the graph shows a continuous downward slope — it is downhill all the way.
- That part of the route does not have many uphills.
Teaching point: A falling line on an elevation graph means downhill running, which is faster and less tiring, so the average speed over that section is the highest of the day.
subQuestions.topic: Data handling – Interpreting an elevation graph

subQuestions.questionText:
The elevation map for **Day 2** of the Leopard Trail Run plots the height above sea level against the distance run. The vertical axis has gridlines labelled 864 m; 900 m; 975 m; 1 050 m and 1 173 m. The horizontal axis is marked at 2,5 km; 5 km; 7,5 km; 10 km; 12,5 km; 15 km; 17,5 km; 20 km and ends at 21,9 km.

Readings from the Day 2 profile:

| Position on the trail | Height above sea level |
|---|---|
| At the 12,5 km mark (highest point) | 1 173 m |
| At the 17,5 km mark (second peak) | 1 050 m |
| At the end of the trail (21,9 km) | 900 m |

John stated that on Day 2, while he was running from the 17,5 km mark to the end of the trail, he had moved more than 100 metres closer to sea level.

Show, by means of calculations, whether or not he is correct.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: Difference in height $= 1\,050 \text{ m} - 900 \text{ m}$ (1RT 1st correct value read at 17,5 km; 1RT 2nd correct value read at the end of the trail)
Mark 3: $= 150 \text{ m}$, and since $150 \text{ m} > 100 \text{ m}$, he is **CORRECT** (1O conclusion)
Teaching point: 'Closer to sea level' means the height DROPPED, so subtract the ending height from the starting height. Then compare your answer with the 100 m in the claim before writing the conclusion.
subQuestions.topic: Data handling – Reading and comparing graph values

questions.title: Classroom reading corner: pillow storage bags, circular birthday tags and packets of sweets

subQuestions.questionText:
Mrs Kgomo is a Grade 2 teacher at Happy Valley Primary School. She has a reading corner at the back of her classroom, where learners who wait for their transport after school sit and read a book.

The school day ends at 12:55.

Tendani's father was late and only came to fetch him at 14:13.

Determine how long Tendani sat in the reading corner.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $= 14{:}13 - 12{:}55$ (1MA subtracting the times)
Mark 2: $= 1$ hour 18 minutes (1A simplification)
Also accept: 78 minutes OR 1,3 hours (AO — answer only gets full marks)
Teaching point: Work in two steps: from 12:55 to 13:55 is 1 hour, and from 13:55 to 14:13 is a further 18 minutes, giving 1 h 18 min. Remember an hour has 60 minutes, not 100.

subQuestions.questionText:
Mrs Kgomo stores pillows in bags. Learners sit on these pillows after school.

**DIMENSIONS OF THE BAG**

| Dimension | Measurement |
|---|---|
| Length | 46 cm |
| Width (depth) | 30 cm |
| Height | 48 cm |

Through the see-through panel on the front of the bag you can see that ONE bag holds **FOUR pillows**, stacked one on top of the other.

The height of one pillow is 11 cm.

Determine the difference between the total height of the pillows in ONE bag and the height of the bag.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Total height of the 4 pillows $= 11 \text{ cm} \times 4$ (1MA multiplying by 4)
Mark 2: $= 44 \text{ cm}$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 3: Difference $= 48 \text{ cm} - 44 \text{ cm}$ (1RT height of the bag read from the dimensions)
Mark 4: $= 4 \text{ cm}$ (1CA simplification)

OR

Mark 1: Difference $= 48 \text{ cm} - 11 \text{ cm} - 11 \text{ cm} - 11 \text{ cm} - 11 \text{ cm}$ (1RT height; 1MA subtracting 11 cm; 1MA subtracting all four 11's)
Mark 4: $= 4 \text{ cm}$ (1CA simplification; AO)

Teaching point: Choose the correct dimension of the bag — the pillows are stacked vertically, so you must compare them with the HEIGHT (48 cm), not the length or width.

subQuestions.questionText:
Mrs Kgomo stores pillows in rectangular bags. Piping (thin cord covered in fabric used to decorate the bag and reinforce the seams) runs around the bottom edge of each bag.

**DIMENSIONS OF THE BAG**

| Dimension | Measurement |
|---|---|
| Length | 46 cm |
| Width (depth) | 30 cm |
| Height | 48 cm |

The piping around the bottom edge of some of the bags needs to be replaced. The store sells the piping in half-metre lengths.

Calculate the total length of piping she will have to purchase to replace the piping around the bottom edges of FOUR bags.

You may use the following formula:

**Perimeter = 2 (length + width)**
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Perimeter $= 2(46 \text{ cm} + 30 \text{ cm})$ (1SF correct substitution)
Mark 2: $= 2(76 \text{ cm}) = 152 \text{ cm}$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 3: Total length for 4 bags $= 152 \times 4 = 608 \text{ cm}$ (1MA multiplying by 4)
Mark 4: $= \dfrac{608}{100} = 6{,}08 \text{ m}$ (1C converting to metres)
Mark 5: $\therefore$ she must buy **6,5 m** (1R correct rounding — up to the next half-metre)

OR (working in metres from the start)

Mark 1: $30 \text{ cm} = 0{,}3 \text{ m}$ and $46 \text{ cm} = 0{,}46 \text{ m}$ (1C metres)
Mark 2: Perimeter $= 2(0{,}3 \text{ m} + 0{,}46 \text{ m})$ (1SF correct substitution)
Mark 3: $= 1{,}52 \text{ m}$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 4: Total $= 1{,}52 \text{ m} \times 4 = 6{,}08 \text{ m}$ (1MCA multiplying by 4)
Mark 5: $\therefore$ she must buy **6,5 m** (1R correct rounding)

OR (counting half-metre lengths)

Mark 1: Perimeter $= 2(46 \text{ cm} + 30 \text{ cm})$ (1SF)
Mark 2: $= 152 \text{ cm}$ (1CA)
Mark 3: Total for 4 bags $= 152 \times 4 = 608 \text{ cm}$ (1MA)
Mark 4: $\tfrac{1}{2}\text{ m} = 50 \text{ cm}$ (1C to centimetres)
Mark 5: Number of half-metre lengths $= 608 \div 50 = 12{,}16 \approx \mathbf{13}$ lengths (1R correct rounding)

Teaching point: The piping is sold only in half-metre lengths, so you must round UP to the next half-metre — 6,08 m becomes 6,5 m (13 half-metre lengths). Rounding down would leave part of a bag without piping.

subQuestions.questionText:
Mrs Kgomo created a birthday calendar for her 2024 class to hang against the wall. She will write each learner's name and birthday on a small circular wooden tag and attach the tag to the correct month.

The circular wooden tag has a **diameter of 8 cm**. Near the top of the tag there is a small circular hole (used to attach a ring for hanging the tag); the area of this circular hole is 0,3142 cm².

Determine, in cm, the circumference of the circular wooden tag.

You may use the following formula:

**Circumference of a circle = 3,142 × diameter**
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Circumference $= 3{,}142 \times 8 \text{ cm}$ (1SF substituting the diameter)
Mark 2: $= 25{,}136 \text{ cm}$ (1A simplification; NPR; AO)
Teaching point: The formula uses the DIAMETER (the full width across the circle, 8 cm here) — do not halve it first, that is only needed when a formula asks for the radius.

subQuestions.questionText:
A circular wooden tag used on Mrs Kgomo's birthday calendar measures **8 cm across** (its diameter is 8 cm, as shown on both the height and the width of the diagram of the tag).

Determine, in cm, the radius of ONE circular wooden tag.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Radius $= \dfrac{8 \text{ cm}}{2}$ (1MA concept of radius)
Mark 2: $= 4 \text{ cm}$ (1A simplification; NPU; AO)
Teaching point: The radius is the distance from the centre to the edge, which is always HALF the diameter.

subQuestions.questionText:
Every year Mrs Kgomo paints the front surface area of the circular wooden tags for her birthday calendar.

- Each circular wooden tag has a diameter of 8 cm, so its **radius is 4 cm**.
- Each tag has a small circular hole (for the hanging ring) with an area of **0,3142 cm²**. This hole is not painted.
- The spread rate of the paint is **6 m²/ℓ**.
- The hardware store sells paint in 50 mℓ, 1 litre, 5 litre and 20 litre containers.

Mrs Kgomo claims that a 50 mℓ can of paint will be sufficient to paint ONE side of 36 circular wooden tags.

Verify her statement. Show ALL calculations.

Use the following formula:

**Area of a circle = 3,142 × radius²**
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Area of a circle $= 3{,}142 \times (4 \text{ cm})^2$ (1SF correct substitution)
Mark 2: $= 3{,}142 \times 16 \text{ cm}^2$ (1MCA squaring)
Mark 3: $= 50{,}272 \text{ cm}^2$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 4: Area to be painted per tag $= 50{,}272 - 0{,}3142 = 49{,}9578 \text{ cm}^2$ (1CA difference)
Mark 5: Total area $= 36 \times 49{,}9578 = 1\,798{,}4808 \text{ cm}^2$ (1MCA multiplying by 36)
Mark 6: Total area in m² $= 1\,798{,}4808 \div 100^2 = 0{,}179848 \text{ m}^2$ (1C dividing by 10 000)
Mark 7: $6 \text{ m}^2 = 1 \text{ }\ell = 1\,000 \text{ m}\ell$, so $50 \text{ m}\ell$ covers $0{,}3 \text{ m}^2$ (1MA using the ratio)
Mark 8: $0{,}3 \text{ m}^2 > 0{,}179848 \text{ m}^2$ (1CA comparing the areas)
Mark 9: Therefore 50 mℓ will be **more than sufficient** — her statement is VALID (1O verification)

OR (working out how much paint is actually needed)

Marks 1–6 as above, then:
Mark 7: $n = \dfrac{0{,}17984808}{6} \text{ }\ell$ (1MCA using the ratio)
Mark 8: $= 0{,}02997466 \text{ }\ell \approx 30 \text{ m}\ell$ (1CA paint needed)
Mark 9: $30 \text{ m}\ell < 50 \text{ m}\ell$, so the statement is **VALID** (1O verification)

OR (working entirely in cm²)

Mark 1: $3{,}142 \times 4^2$ (1SF)
Mark 2: $= 3{,}142 \times 16$ (1MCA squaring)
Mark 3: $= 50{,}272 \text{ cm}^2$ (1CA)
Mark 4: $50{,}272 - 0{,}3142 = 49{,}9578 \text{ cm}^2$ (1CA difference)
Mark 5: $6 \text{ m}^2/\ell = 60\,000 \text{ cm}^2 / 1\,000 \text{ m}\ell$ (1C conversion)
Mark 6: Paint for one tag $= 49{,}9578 \div 60\,000 \times 1\,000 = 0{,}83263 \text{ m}\ell$ (1MCA using the ratio)
Mark 7 & 8: Paint for 36 tags $= 0{,}83263 \times 36 = 29{,}97468 \approx 30 \text{ m}\ell$ (1MCA multiplying by 36; 1CA paint needed)
Mark 9: **VALID** (1O verification)

Teaching point: Three traps here — (1) subtract the hole before multiplying by 36, (2) the spread rate is in m² but the tags are in cm², so you must convert ($1 \text{ m}^2 = 100^2 = 10\,000 \text{ cm}^2$), and (3) finish with a written conclusion comparing your answer to the 50 mℓ can.
subQuestions.topic: Measurement – Area, spread rate and verification

subQuestions.questionText:
On each learner's birthday, the learner receives a cubic-shaped packet of homemade sweets. A cube has all three dimensions (length, width and height) equal.

The volume of the cubic-shaped packet is 2 744 cm³.

Calculate the side length of the cubic-shaped packet.

You may use the following formula:

**Volume of a cube = side × side × side**
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: $2\,744 \text{ cm}^3 = \text{side} \times \text{side} \times \text{side}$ (1SF substituting the number; 1SF cube unit)
Mark 3: $(\text{side})^3 = 2\,744 \text{ cm}^3$ (1MA changing the subject of the formula)
Mark 4: $14 \times 14 \times 14 = 2\,744$, so side $= 14 \text{ cm}$ (1CA simplification)
Teaching point: You are working BACKWARDS from the volume, so you need the cube root of 2 744. On a calculator use the $\sqrt[3]{\;}$ key, or test values: $10^3 = 1\,000$ (too small), $15^3 = 3\,375$ (too big), $14^3 = 2\,744$ (correct).

subQuestions.questionText:
Each learner receives a cubic-shaped packet containing 35 different coloured sweets.

TABLE 2 below shows the number of sweets per colour.

**TABLE 2: NUMBER OF SWEETS PER COLOUR**

| Colour of sweets | Number of sweets |
|---|---|
| Blue | 4 |
| Purple | 5 |
| Pink | 8 |
| Orange | 11 |
| Yellow | 7 |

Determine the probability, as a decimal, of randomly choosing a pink or a yellow sweet from the packet.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Favourable outcomes $= 8 + 7 = 15$ (1A numerator)
Mark 2: Total number of sweets $= 35$ (1A denominator)
Mark 3: $P = \dfrac{15}{35} = 0{,}42857\ldots \approx 0{,}43$ (1CA simplification; NPR)

OR

Mark 1 & 2: $P = \dfrac{8}{35} + \dfrac{7}{35}$ (1A denominator; 1A writing as decimals)
Mark 3: $= 0{,}22857\ldots + 0{,}2 = 0{,}42857\ldots \approx 0{,}43$ (1CA simplification)

Teaching point: The word 'or' means you ADD the two favourable groups together before dividing by the total of 35.

questions.title: Crude oil distillation tower and replacing garage doors with double-brick walls

subQuestions.questionText:
Crude oil is heated in a vertical, cylindrical tower to separate and extract products such as petroleum gas, gasoline (petrol), kerosene (lamp oil), diesel, industrial oil and paraffin wax, which boil at different temperatures.

The tower diagram shows the products and the temperatures at which they are drawn off, working from the TOP of the tower downwards:

| Position in the tower (top to bottom) | Temperature | Product extracted |
|---|---|---|
| Top | 20 °C | Petroleum gas |
| | 150 °C | Gasoline (petrol) |
| | 200 °C | Kerosene (lamp oil) |
| | 300 °C | Diesel |
| | 370 °C | Industrial oil |
| Bottom (furnace end) | 400 °C | Paraffin wax |

NOTE: Extraction occurs because different liquids have different boiling points.

Identify the crude oil product that will be third to boil.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **Kerosene (lamp oil)** (2RT correct product)
Teaching point: 'Third to boil' means the third-LOWEST boiling temperature. Put the temperatures in order: 20 °C (petroleum gas), 150 °C (gasoline), then 200 °C (kerosene) — the third one.
subQuestions.topic: Data handling – Ordering values in context

subQuestions.questionText:
Crude oil is heated in a vertical, cylindrical tower to separate and extract different products. The tower diagram shows the temperature at which each product is drawn off:

| Temperature | Product extracted |
|---|---|
| 20 °C | Petroleum gas |
| 150 °C | Gasoline (petrol) |
| 200 °C | Kerosene (lamp oil) |
| 300 °C | Diesel |
| 370 °C | Industrial oil |
| 400 °C | Paraffin wax |

Write down the product extracted at 150 °C.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **Gasoline (petrol)** (2RT correct product)
Teaching point: Find 150 °C in the temperature column and read straight across to the product named next to it.

subQuestions.questionText:
In the crude oil distillation tower, the products are drawn off at these boiling temperatures:

| Temperature | Product extracted |
|---|---|
| 20 °C | Petroleum gas |
| 150 °C | Gasoline (petrol) |
| 200 °C | Kerosene (lamp oil) |
| 300 °C | Diesel |
| 370 °C | Industrial oil |
| 400 °C | Paraffin wax |

Convert the boiling point of diesel to degrees Fahrenheit.

Use the formula: $^{\circ}\text{C} = \dfrac{(^{\circ}\text{F} - 32)}{1{,}8}$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Boiling point of diesel $= 300\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$ (1RT correct value)
Mark 2: $300 = \dfrac{(^{\circ}\text{F} - 32)}{1{,}8}$ (1SF substituting the information correctly)
Mark 3: $^{\circ}\text{F} = 1{,}8 \times 300 + 32$ (1S changing the subject of the formula)
Mark 4: $= 572\ ^{\circ}\text{F}$ (1CA simplification; AO)
Teaching point: The formula gives °C in terms of °F, but you need °F. Rearrange it: multiply both sides by 1,8 and then add 32.

subQuestions.questionText:
Crude oil extraction takes place in a large, vertical, cylindrical tower. The diagram of the tower divides it into three parts:

- **A** — the domed top of the tower
- **B** — the straight cylindrical middle section, with a height of **54 m**
- **C** — the domed bottom of the tower

Other information:
- The tower has a **diameter of 6 m**.
- The total surface area of sections (A + C) = **150,816 m²**.
- The pipes leading in and out of the tower take up **2,5%** of the surface area of part B.

Calculate the total surface area of the vertical, cylindrical tower, excluding the area taken up by the pipes.

Use the formula:

**Surface area of an open cylinder = 3,142 × diameter × height**
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Surface area of part B $= 3{,}142 \times 6 \text{ m} \times 54 \text{ m}$ (1SF substitution)
Mark 2: $= 1\,018{,}008 \text{ m}^2$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 3: Area of pipes $= \dfrac{2{,}5}{100} \times \dfrac{1\,018{,}008}{1}$ (1MCA percentage calculation)
Mark 4: $= 25{,}4502 \text{ m}^2$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 5 & 6: Total surface area $= 1\,018{,}008 \text{ m}^2 - 25{,}4502 \text{ m}^2 + 150{,}816 \text{ m}^2$ (1MCA subtracting the pipe area; 1MA adding A + C)
Mark 7: $= 1\,143{,}3738 \text{ m}^2$ (1CA total surface area)

OR (using 97,5% directly)

Mark 1: $= 3{,}142 \times 6 \text{ m} \times 54 \text{ m}$ (1SF substitution)
Mark 2: $= 1\,018{,}008 \text{ m}^2$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 3 & 4: Area excluding pipes $= \dfrac{97{,}5}{100} \times \dfrac{1\,018{,}008}{1}$ (1MA less 2,5%; 1MCA percentage calculation)
Mark 5: $= 992{,}5578 \text{ m}^2$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 6: Total SA $= 992{,}5578 \text{ m}^2 + 150{,}816 \text{ m}^2$ (1MA adding A + C)
Mark 7: $= 1\,143{,}3738 \text{ m}^2$ (1CA total surface area; NPR)

Teaching point: Do the calculation in three stages — the curved side (part B), then remove the 2,5% for the pipes, then add the given area of the two domed ends (A + C). Only part B loses area to the pipes.
subQuestions.topic: Measurement – Surface area of a cylinder and percentages

subQuestions.questionText:
A worker at the oil refinery intends converting her double-door garage into a bigger living room by building double-bricked walls to replace both of the doors.

The diagram showing the pattern of how the bricks should be laid (with the first two rows completed) gives the following counts for filling ONE garage-door opening:

| Read from the brick pattern diagram | Value |
|---|---|
| Bricks in ONE row of the double-brick wall | 19 |
| Number of rows (layers) of bricks needed to fill one door opening | 20 |
| (Counted as two separate single walls: bricks per single row) | 10 |

There are TWO garage doors to be replaced.

NOTE:
- 525 bricks per pallet at a price of R6,45 per brick. Bricks are sold per pallet.
- Half bricks are thrown away (not re-used).

Determine the total number of pallets of bricks needed to replace both garage doors.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: Number of bricks in 1 row of a double-brick wall $= 19$ (2RT bricks in a double row)
Mark 3: Number of bricks for 1 garage door $= 19 \times 20 = 380$ (1A number of layers)
Mark 4: Total number of bricks needed $= 380 \times 2 = 760$ (1MCA doubling for the two doors)
Mark 5: $760 \div 525 = 1{,}45\ldots \therefore$ **2 pallets** of bricks (1R number of pallets)

OR (counting the two brick skins separately)

Mark 1 & 2: Single line wall $= 20 \times 10 = 200$ bricks (1RT bricks (height); 1RT bricks (row))
Mark 3: Double line wall $= 2 \times 200 = 400$ bricks (1CA bricks on a double wall)
Mark 4: For two garage doors $= 2 \times 400 = 800$ bricks (1MCA doubling)
Mark 5: $\therefore$ **2 pallets** (1R number of pallets)

Teaching point: Bricks are only sold per full pallet, so you must round UP — 760 (or 800) bricks needs 2 pallets, because 1 pallet holds only 525 bricks.

subQuestions.questionText:
A worker is replacing BOTH doors of her double garage with double-brick walls.

- The opening of a garage door has dimensions of **2,13 m × 3 m**.
- **2 pallets** of bricks are needed for the job. There are **525 bricks per pallet at R6,45 per brick**, and bricks are sold per pallet.

Other costs to build the double-brick wall:
- Material, other than bricks, cost R2 000,00
- Labour is R500,00 per square metre

The owner states that the total cost to replace both garage doors with walls would be R15 200,00.

Verify her statement by means of calculations.

You may use the following formula: **Area = length × width**
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: Area of 2 doors $= 2 \times 2{,}13 \times 3$ (1MA doubling; 1SF correct values)
Mark 3: $= 12{,}78 \text{ m}^2$ (1A simplification)
Mark 4: Labour cost $= 12{,}78 \text{ m}^2 \times \text{R}500 = \text{R}6\,390$ (1CA labour cost)
Mark 5: Brick cost $= 2 \times 525 \times \text{R}6{,}45 = \text{R}6\,772{,}50$ (1CA brick cost)
Mark 6: Total cost $= \text{R}2\,000 + \text{R}6\,390 + \text{R}6\,772{,}50 = \text{R}15\,162{,}50$ (1CA amount)
Mark 7: The statement is **NOT VALID** — the actual total is R15 162,50, not R15 200,00 (1O verification)

OR (one door at a time)

Mark 1: Area of one door $= 2{,}13 \text{ m} \times 3 \text{ m}$ (1SF correct values)
Mark 2: $= 6{,}39 \text{ m}^2$ (1A simplification)
Mark 3: Labour $= 6{,}39 \text{ m}^2 \times \text{R}500 = \text{R}3\,195$ (1MCA labour cost)
Mark 4: For two doors $= 2 \times \text{R}3\,195 = \text{R}6\,390$ (1CA doubling)
Mark 5: Cost per pallet $= \text{R}6{,}45 \times 525 = \text{R}3\,386{,}25$; for two pallets $= \text{R}6\,772{,}50$ (1CA brick cost)
Mark 6: Total $= \text{R}2\,000 + \text{R}6\,390 + \text{R}6\,772{,}50 = \text{R}15\,162{,}50$ (1CA amount)
Mark 7: **NOT VALID** (1O verification)

Teaching point: A 'verify' question needs THREE things — the full working, the calculated answer, and a written statement saying whether the claim is right or wrong. R15 162,50 is close to R15 200,00 but not equal to it, so the statement is not valid.

subQuestions.questionText:
Bricks for the double-brick wall are delivered stacked on a wooden pallet, with 525 bricks per pallet at R6,45 per brick. Bricks are sold per pallet.

Give ONE suitable reason why the bricks have to be placed on a wooden pallet.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: Any ONE suitable reason (2O reason), for example:
- So that they can easily be lifted by a forklift.
- Storage, loading and transportation are made easier.
- It keeps the bricks from breaking / protects them from damage.
- It makes counting the bricks easier.
- It keeps the stack tight and compact.
Teaching point: Link your reason to how the bricks are actually handled — moved, stored, counted or protected.

questions.title: Road trip around Australia: distances and driving times, the height of Uluru, and state area sizes

subQuestions.questionText:
Chris and Boipelo are planning a year-long trip, mostly along the A1 motorway, around Australia. It is the world's longest continuous road of 14 655 km that passes through every state and connects seven of its eight capitals.

ANNEXURE C gives the distances and driving times between the major cities on the map of Australia:

| Route between cities | Distance | Driving time |
|---|---|---|
| Perth – Broome | 2 811 km | 30 hours |
| Broome – Darwin | 1 871 km | 21 h 13 min |
| Darwin – Cairns | 2 850 km | 33 h 55 min |
| Cairns – Brisbane | 1 705 km | 20 h 40 min |
| Brisbane – Sydney | 922 km | 10 h 30 min |
| Sydney – Melbourne | 1 062 km | 13 h 40 min |
| Melbourne – Adelaide | 738 km | 9 h 6 min |
| Darwin – Adelaide (inland route) | 3 027 km | 35 hours |
| Perth – Adelaide | (not given) | 29 hours |

Write down the names of the cities where the distance between them is 738 km.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **Adelaide and Melbourne** (1RT 1st city; 1RT 2nd city)
Teaching point: Find 738 km in the distance column and read off BOTH cities that the arrow joins — a distance always belongs to a pair of places.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Reading distances from a map

subQuestions.questionText:
Chris and Boipelo are planning a year-long trip around Australia. ANNEXURE C includes a map of their planned trip, with a month label and an arrow placed at each stage of the route.

The states and territories of Australia are laid out as follows:
- **Western Australia** takes up the whole western third of the country.
- The **Northern Territory** and **South Australia** form the central strip (Northern Territory in the north, South Australia in the south).
- **Queensland** is the north-east, **New South Wales** the east, **Victoria** the south-eastern corner and **Tasmania** the island south of Victoria.

The month labels are placed around the map in this order:

| Month | Position on the planned-trip map |
|---|---|
| JAN | On the eastern coast |
| FEB | On the island to the far south |
| MAR | Back on the mainland, in the south-eastern corner |
| APR | Up the north-eastern coast |
| MAY | Across the far north of the central strip |
| JUN | Heading west through the central north |
| JUL | At the north-western corner of the central strip |
| AUG | Part-way down the north-west coast |
| SEP | On the mid-west coast |
| OCT | In the far south-west corner |
| NOV | Along the southern coast of the western third, heading east |
| DEC | In the centre of the country, heading back north-east |

Name the FOUR months when Chris and Boipelo will be in Western Australia.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: 1st correct month (1RT)
Mark 2: 2nd correct month (1RT)
Mark 3: ALL correct months (1RT)
Answer: **August, September, October and November** (Aug, Sep, Oct, Nov)
Teaching point: First locate the border of Western Australia on the map, then list only the month labels that fall INSIDE it. July is still on the Northern Territory side of the border, and December has already crossed into South Australia.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Interpreting a route map

subQuestions.questionText:
The A1 motorway is the world's longest continuous road, at **14 655 km**, and it forms a complete loop around Australia. Chris and Boipelo will drive the whole loop.

The distances between the cities along the A1 loop are given on ANNEXURE C:

| Route between cities | Distance | Driving time |
|---|---|---|
| Perth – Broome | 2 811 km | 30 hours |
| Broome – Darwin | 1 871 km | 21 h 13 min |
| Darwin – Cairns | 2 850 km | 33 h 55 min |
| Cairns – Brisbane | 1 705 km | 20 h 40 min |
| Brisbane – Sydney | 922 km | 10 h 30 min |
| Sydney – Melbourne | 1 062 km | 13 h 40 min |
| Melbourne – Adelaide | 738 km | 9 h 6 min |
| Adelaide – Perth | (not given) | 29 hours |

(The inland route from Darwin to Adelaide, 3 027 km in 35 hours, is a short cut across the middle and is NOT part of the A1 loop.)

Determine the distance from Perth to Adelaide.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $14\,655 - (738 + 1\,062 + 922 + 1\,705 + 2\,850 + 1\,871 + 2\,811)$ (1RT all correct values)
Mark 2: $= 14\,655 - 11\,959$ (1MCA subtracting)
Mark 3: $= 2\,696 \text{ km}$ (1CA simplification; AO)
Teaching point: Because the A1 is a closed loop, the missing leg equals the total length of the loop minus all the legs that ARE given. Do not include the 3 027 km inland Darwin–Adelaide route — that is a different road across the middle.

subQuestions.questionText:
Chris and Boipelo's planned-trip map places a month label at each stage of their year-long journey around Australia.

The states and territories are laid out as follows: Western Australia in the west; Northern Territory and South Australia in the central strip; Queensland in the north-east; New South Wales in the east; Victoria in the south-eastern corner; and **Tasmania**, the island lying south of Victoria across the Bass Strait.

On the planned-trip map, the **FEB** label and arrow are placed on the island to the far south, off the south-eastern corner of the mainland.

Name the state where they plan to be during February.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **Tasmania** (2RT correct state)
Teaching point: Match the position of the month label to the state names given on the map of Australia — the only Australian state that is an island south of the mainland is Tasmania.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Locating places on a map

subQuestions.questionText:
The distances and driving times between the major Australian cities are given on ANNEXURE C:

| Route between cities | Distance | Driving time |
|---|---|---|
| Perth – Broome | 2 811 km | 30 hours |
| Broome – Darwin | 1 871 km | 21 h 13 min |
| Darwin – Cairns | 2 850 km | 33 h 55 min |
| Cairns – Brisbane | 1 705 km | 20 h 40 min |
| Brisbane – Sydney | 922 km | 10 h 30 min |
| Sydney – Melbourne | 1 062 km | 13 h 40 min |
| Melbourne – Adelaide | 738 km | 9 h 6 min |

Calculate the average speed, in km/h, from Brisbane to Cairns.

You may use the following formula: **Distance = speed × time**
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $1\,705 \text{ km} = s \times 20 \text{ h } 40 \text{ min}$ (1SF substitution)
Mark 2: $1\,705 \text{ km} = s \times 20{,}67 \text{ h}$ (1C converting the minutes to hours: $40 \div 60 = 0{,}67$)
Mark 3: Speed $= \dfrac{1\,705 \text{ km}}{20{,}67 \text{ h}}$ (1S changing the subject of the formula)
Mark 4: $= 82{,}5 \text{ km/h}$ (1CA simplification)
Teaching point: Speed is measured in km per HOUR, so 20 h 40 min must first be written as a decimal number of hours — divide the 40 minutes by 60 to get 0,67 h.

subQuestions.questionText:
Chris and Boipelo plan to visit Uluru. This oval-shaped big rock rises **1 142 feet** above the surrounding desert plain.

A diagram compares the height of Uluru with some other tourist attractions around the world. The heights labelled on the diagram are:

| Attraction | Height on the diagram |
|---|---|
| Sydney Harbour Bridge | 134 m |
| **ULURU** | **348 m** |
| The Eiffel Tower | 324 m |
| The Great Pyramid of Giza | 139 m |
| Big Ben | 96 m |

Determine, rounded to THREE decimal places, the conversion factor from feet to metres used in this diagram, in the form 1 foot = … m.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: $1\,142 \text{ feet} = 348 \text{ m}$ (1RT reading 1 142; 1RT reading 348)
Mark 3: $1 \text{ foot} = \dfrac{348}{1\,142} = 0{,}304728546\ldots \approx \mathbf{0{,}305 \text{ m}}$ (1A correct value to three decimal places)
Teaching point: You are told the SAME height in two units, so divide the metre value by the foot value to find what ONE foot is worth in metres.

subQuestions.questionText:
A diagram compares the height of Uluru with some other tourist attractions around the world. The heights labelled on the diagram are:

| Attraction | Height on the diagram |
|---|---|
| Sydney Harbour Bridge | 134 m |
| ULURU | 348 m |
| The Eiffel Tower | 324 m |
| The Great Pyramid of Giza | 139 m |
| Big Ben | 96 m |

Write, as a simplified ratio, the heights of Uluru : Eiffel Tower : Big Ben.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Uluru : Eiffel Tower : Big Ben $= 348 : 324 : 96$ (1RT correct values)
Mark 2: values placed in the correct order (1A correct order)
Mark 3 & 4: divide every part by 12: $= \mathbf{29 : 27 : 8}$ (2CA simplified ratio)
Teaching point: Simplify a three-part ratio by dividing EVERY part by the same number — here the highest common factor of 348, 324 and 96 is 12. Keep the parts in the order named in the question, and a ratio has no units.

subQuestions.questionText:
In addition to the mainland, Australia is surrounded by many thousands of small islands. TABLE 3 gives the areas for the mainland, islands and total for each state or territory. Some values have been omitted.

**TABLE 3: AREA SIZES OF THE MAINLAND, ISLANDS AND TOTAL FOR EACH STATE OR TERRITORY**

| State / Territory | Mainland area (km²) | Island area (km²) | Total area (km²) | Percentage of total area |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Western Australia | 2 526 924 | 3 089 | 2 527 013 | 32,9 |
| Queensland | 1 723 030 | 6 712 | 1 729 742 | 22,5 |
| Northern Territory | 1 334 404 | 13 387 | 1 347 791 | 17,5 |
| South Australia | 979 651 | 4 670 | 984 321 | 12,8 |
| New South Wales | 801 137 | 13 | 801 150 | 10,4 |
| Victoria | 227 038 | 406 | 227 444 | 3,0 |
| Tasmania | 64 519 | 3 882 | 68 401 | 0,9 |
| Australian Capital Territory | 2 358 | – | 2 358 | – |
| **TOTAL (AUSTRALIA)** | **7 656 061** | **32 159** | **7 688 220** | … |

A meteorite (rock from the sky) fell somewhere in Australia.

Write down the probability that it randomly fell in Queensland.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: $P = 22{,}5\%$ (2A correct probability)

OR

$P = \dfrac{1\,729\,742}{7\,688\,220} = 0{,}224986\ldots$ or $22{,}5\%$ (2A correct probability)

Teaching point: The table already gives Queensland's share of the total area as 22,5%, so that percentage IS the probability. If you calculate it yourself, use the TOTAL area of Queensland over the TOTAL area of Australia.

subQuestions.questionText:
TABLE 3 gives the areas for the mainland, islands and total for each Australian state or territory.

**TABLE 3: AREA SIZES OF THE MAINLAND, ISLANDS AND TOTAL FOR EACH STATE OR TERRITORY**

| State / Territory | Mainland area (km²) | Island area (km²) | Total area (km²) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Western Australia | 2 526 924 | 3 089 | 2 527 013 |
| Queensland | 1 723 030 | 6 712 | 1 729 742 |
| Northern Territory | 1 334 404 | 13 387 | 1 347 791 |
| South Australia | 979 651 | 4 670 | 984 321 |
| New South Wales | 801 137 | 13 | 801 150 |
| Victoria | 227 038 | 406 | 227 444 |
| Tasmania | 64 519 | 3 882 | 68 401 |
| Australian Capital Territory | 2 358 | – | 2 358 |
| **TOTAL (AUSTRALIA)** | **7 656 061** | **32 159** | **7 688 220** |

Show, with calculations, why it could be stated that the total area of the islands of Australia is approximately half of the area of the mainland area of Tasmania.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: $\dfrac{\text{Area of islands}}{\text{Mainland area of Tasmania}} = \dfrac{32\,159}{64\,519}$ (1RT area of islands; 1RT area of Tasmania)
Mark 3: $= 0{,}498 \approx 0{,}5$, i.e. approximately half (1CA simplification)

OR

Mark 1 & 2: Half of Tasmania $= 64\,519 \times \tfrac{1}{2} = 32\,259{,}5 \text{ km}^2$ (1RT Tasmania area; 1MA simplification), and the islands $= 32\,159 \text{ km}^2$ (1RT island area), which is very close to 32 259,5 km².

OR

Mark 1 & 2: $64\,519 : 32\,159$ (1RT area of islands; 1RT area of Tasmania)
Mark 3: $\approx 2 : 1$ (1CA simplification)

Teaching point: 'Show why' means you must produce the numbers — read the TOTAL island area (32 159 km²) and the MAINLAND area of Tasmania (64 519 km²) and then either divide, halve, or write them as a ratio.
subQuestions.topic: Data handling – Comparing values from a table

subQuestions.label: 5.3.3 (a)
subQuestions.questionText:
TABLE 3 gives the area sizes for each Australian state or territory. The row for the Australian Capital Territory reads:

| State / Territory | Mainland area (km²) | Island area (km²) | Total area (km²) | Percentage of total area |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Australian Capital Territory | 2 358 | – | 2 358 | – |
| **TOTAL (AUSTRALIA)** | **7 656 061** | **32 159** | **7 688 220** | … |

NOTE: Territory – a big area that compares to a district or province.

The Australian Capital Territory has a population of 454 499.

Determine, rounded to the nearest whole number, the population density of the Australian Capital Territory as people per square km.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: Population density $= \dfrac{454\,499}{2\,358}$ (1RT correct population 454 499; 1RT correct area 2 358)
Mark 3: $= 192{,}747\ldots \approx \mathbf{193}$ people per km² (1R simplification, rounded)
Teaching point: Population density $= \dfrac{\text{number of people}}{\text{area in km}^2}$. Population always goes on TOP — swapping them gives a meaningless tiny answer.

subQuestions.label: 5.3.3 (b)
subQuestions.questionText:
TABLE 3 gives the area sizes for each Australian state or territory, and the last column gives each one's percentage of the total area of Australia:

| State / Territory | Total area (km²) | Percentage of total area |
|---|---|---|
| Western Australia | 2 527 013 | 32,9 |
| Queensland | 1 729 742 | 22,5 |
| Northern Territory | 1 347 791 | 17,5 |
| South Australia | 984 321 | 12,8 |
| New South Wales | 801 150 | 10,4 |
| Victoria | 227 444 | 3,0 |
| Tasmania | 68 401 | 0,9 |
| Australian Capital Territory | 2 358 | – (omitted) |
| **TOTAL (AUSTRALIA)** | **7 688 220** | … |

The percentage of total area for the Australian Capital Territory has been left out of the table.

Give a suitable reason, with calculations, why this area is omitted from the percentage calculation in the table.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: Percentage of land area $= \dfrac{2\,358}{7\,688\,220} \times 100\%$ (1RT correct 2 358; 1RT correct 7 688 220)
Mark 3: $= 0{,}0306\ldots\%$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 4: The percentage rounds off to ZERO (to one decimal place, as used in the rest of the table), so it would show as 0,0 and add nothing to the table (1O opinion)
Teaching point: Every other percentage in the table is given to ONE decimal place. Because 0,0306% rounds to 0,0%, the value is too small to display meaningfully, which is why it was left out.
